title: Four incidents on one Friday
scenario: A studio runs a campaign and a fan site. Four things go wrong on the same day. You choose the first action for each. Use the exhibit. The studio, the log and the numbers are made up for this case. The vendor lines are copied from the docs.
exhibit:
INCIDENT LOG, Friday 2026-09-25 (made up for this case):
  #1  09:10  A design file that is shared publicly contains the studio's OpenAI API key.
  #2  11:40  An approved ad is live with a garbled logo. 4,000 views so far.
  #3  13:00  The video pipeline calls the OpenAI Videos API with sora-2.
             Every call fails.
  #4  15:30  On the fan image site, a user reports an unsafe image made by another
             user. The app sends no safety identifier with its requests.

VENDOR LINES (copied from the docs):
  OpenAI: "If you believe an API key has been exposed, misused, or otherwise compromised, revoke it promptly and replace it with a new key."
  OpenAI deprecations: on March 24th, 2026, developers using the Videos API and Sora 2 models were notified of removal from the API on September 24, 2026. Shutdown date 2026-09-24: Videos API, sora-2, sora-2-pro and their dated snapshots. Recommended replacement: "---".
  OpenAI: safety identifiers give "a stable way to trace activity back to an individual end user". "Hash the username or email address in order to avoid sending us any identifying information."

questions.prompt: What is the first action for incident #1, the key in a public file?

options.text: Wait until the end of the day, then change the key on the normal schedule
options.explanation: The key is exposed now, so the harm is live. The OpenAI docs say to revoke it promptly.

options.text: Delete the design file and keep the key, because nobody has copied it yet
options.explanation: The studio cannot know who has copied it. Deleting the file does not make the key safe again.

options.text: Revoke the key and replace it with a new one, then check what it was used for
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say to revoke a compromised key promptly and replace it. The usage page shows what the key did.

options.text: Make a new key now and keep the old key active for a week as a safety net
options.explanation: A slow handover fits a normal rotation. With a leak, the old key must stop working at once.

questions.prompt: What is the first action for incident #2, the garbled logo in a live ad?

options.text: Find out how the logo was garbled before touching the ad, so the fix is exact
options.explanation: Finding the cause can take a long time. The ad keeps reaching people meanwhile.

options.text: Leave it live until the Monday review, because 4,000 views is a small number
options.explanation: The number does not make the wrong logo acceptable. Stopping the harm comes first.

options.text: Pause the ad and swap in the approved master file, then look for the cause
options.explanation: Right. In this chapter's five steps, contain comes before fix. A kept master makes the swap fast.

options.text: Tell the client in the weekly report, and leave the ad as it is until then
options.explanation: The client and the team should hear about it now, and the ad should be paused.

questions.prompt: What is the right next step for incident #3, the Videos API calls that all fail?

options.text: Retry with growing pauses for a few hours, because the API is most likely overloaded
options.explanation: The API was shut down on the date in the exhibit. No retry can work.

options.text: Stop retrying and move the pipeline to a different video model, then test it
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI listed 2026-09-24 as the shutdown date and gave no replacement, so the studio must pick and test another video model.

options.text: Switch to the preview version of sora-2, which is not part of the shutdown
options.explanation: The exhibit lists sora-2 and its snapshots as removed. There is no exempt preview.

options.text: Ask OpenAI to bring the API back, because the launch depends on this tool
options.explanation: A shutdown after notice is not a fault that support can reverse.

questions.prompt: For incident #4, what should the fan image site have been doing, so that the report can be traced to one user?

options.text: Sending one shared identifier for all fans, so that the logs stay short
options.explanation: A shared identifier cannot trace activity to one user.

options.text: Sending a safety ID made from each fan's hashed email with every request
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say safety identifiers give a stable way to trace activity to one end user, and to hash the email or username.

options.text: Sending each fan's plain email address, so that support can read it easily
options.explanation: The OpenAI docs say to hash it, so no identifying information is sent.

options.text: Sending nothing, because the vendor already knows which fan made each image
options.explanation: The vendor only sees the studio's requests. Without an identifier it cannot tell fans apart.
